newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong rights curbs plan tests Tung leadership.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong rights curbs plan tests Tung leadership.

text.p: A pulse-taking exercise billed as a chance for Hong Kong people to comment on plans to curb their rights has turned into a political storm threatening trust in their future leader, analysts said on Wednesday.

Proposals by future leader Tung Chee-hwa to tighten controls on political groups and protests have thrown into sharp relief questions over his independence after the British colony returns to Chinese rule on July 1, they said.
A three-week consultation on reforms to ban foreign funding for political groups and require police approval for political protests ended on Wednesday.

Opposition from democrats, human rights activists and lawyers has dominated the headlines as responses have poured in, although pro-China parties and unions and business groups have expressed public support.
Tung's aides have declined to say how many of the more than 1,000 responses supported or opposed the proposed curbs.
If Tung proves unwilling to take into account opposing views, he risks being seen as too much Beijing's man and could lose precious credibility among Hong Kong residents, analysts said.
"More and more people are getting distrustful of Mr Tung," said Sing Ming, public administration associate professor at City University.
"Some people are already saying he is just Beijing's 'rubber stamp'," he told Reuters.
Tung proposed the curbs after China's parliament declared parts of the two Public Order and Societies laws incompatible with the Basic Law, Beijing's mini-constitution for Hong Kong.
In a television interview aired on Tuesday, Tung assured his detractors that Hong Kong would never suffer a violent crackdown like China's quashing of pro-democracy protests in June 1989.
Democratic politicians welcomed the pledge, but said it contradicted the proposal to curb protests after July.
Tung and his aides have said the tighter controls on demonstrations and political groups are needed to guarantee political stability after the handover.

Appeals by officials of his future administration for more public support for the proposals raised doubts about the authenticity of the consultation process, political analyst Nihal Jayawickrama said in a telephone interview.
The issue had become a test of Tung's independence and credibility by casting him as too willing to do Beijing's bidding, said Jayawickrama, a law professor at Hong Kong University.
Tung had initially enjoyed both the trust of China and the goodwill of Hong Kong people, but the latter was being eroded by his moves to boost political controls, he said.
"From the time he became chief executive, he has been increasingly speaking the jargon of the Chinese leadership. (That) was not what was expected of him," he said.
"He had... the capacity to act on his own, but he is not doing that, and if he is not doing that then obviously people are going to be increasingly disappointed."

Analysts say the future administration has shown little inclination to make major changes to the proposed reforms, whatever the result of the consultation. "I don't anticipate any dramatic change in the substance of either bill... he might make some cosmetic changes," Jayawickrama said.
The English-language South China Morning Post newspaper said in an editorial that Tung faced his hardest decision and should pay careful heed to concerns and scepticism among the territory's people.
"If he responds to their worries... he can retain the trust that will be such a prop to him in the years ahead," it said.
Tung's aides say they hope to analyse the results of the consultation by mid-May, in time for new laws to be enacted.
But the debate appears unlikely to end then. Lawyers say the laws could breach human rights protection in the Basic Law, making legal challenges likely.
